question: A recent convert reports that she felt the Holy Ghost powerfully testifying to her during the missionary lessons, before her baptism. She is now confused: if the gift of the Holy Ghost is conferred only at confirmation, what did she experience earlier? Which response best reflects official teaching?
choices: Before baptism, the Holy Ghost may give a person occasional manifestations to witness of truth, but the gift of the Holy Ghost bestowed at confirmation conveys the right to His constant companionship, conditioned on continued worthiness.
What she felt was sincere emotion and goodwill; the Holy Ghost does not and cannot operate upon any person until after the ordinance of confirmation is performed.
She received the Holy Ghost permanently at the moment she first believed; the later confirmation is an outward sign that ratifies a sealing already accomplished by faith alone.
Confirmation conveys the Holy Ghost's influence, but the actual 'baptism of fire' is a separate, later spiritual ordinance one must seek and receive independently of confirmation.
The gift, once conferred at confirmation, is an unconditional possession that remains in full regardless of a member's subsequent conduct.
source: D&C 130:23; Bible Dictionary, 'Holy Ghost'; Gospel Topics, 'Holy Ghost'; Acts 10 (Cornelius)
notes: Tests the entitlement-vs-occasional-influence distinction. The 'emotion only' answer over-corrects (the Spirit testifies to investigators); the faith-alone answer is the Protestant trap (no ordinance/authority needed); separating the 'baptism of fire' from confirmation is a near-miss (the baptism of fire IS the gift of the Holy Ghost, D&C 19:31); unconditional retention is folk doctrine ignoring the worthiness condition.

question: In a ward where several youth hold the Aaronic Priesthood, which arrangement for the sacrament is consistent with official policy and the offices defined in D&C 20?
choices: A priest (or a Melchizedek Priesthood holder) may kneel and offer the sacramental prayers; deacons, teachers, and priests may pass it, while teachers and priests may prepare it.
A teacher may offer the sacramental prayers, since the office of teacher outranks that of deacon and includes administering the emblems.
Any baptized member in good standing may bless the bread and water, because the emblems are made sacred by the faith of the congregation rather than by priesthood office.
A deacon may bless the sacrament when no priest is available, provided the bishop authorizes it for that meeting.
Only an ordained priest may handle the sacrament trays at any stage, so deacons must not pass the trays to the congregation.
notes: Tests precise mapping of duties to Aaronic offices. Teacher-blessing inverts the order (priests, not teachers, bless); the 'any member' option is the priesthood-of-all-believers Protestant trap; deacon-blessing-when-no-priest is a folk improvisation contradicting fixed offices; the 'priests only touch trays' option over-restricts (deacons' core duty is passing).

question: Latter-day Saints distinguish the sealing power that binds families eternally from other priesthood authority. According to the Restoration narrative, this sealing power was restored when which heavenly messenger committed his keys, and what scriptural rationale is given for the timing?
choices: Elijah, who appeared in the Kirtland Temple on April 3, 1836, fulfilling Malachi's promise that he would 'turn the heart of the fathers to the children' before the great and dreadful day of the Lord.
Elias, who restored the keys of the Abrahamic covenant in that same vision, since the sealing of families is the renewal of the promises made to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
Moses, who committed the keys of the gathering of Israel, because the sealing of families is the means by which scattered Israel is gathered home.
Peter, James, and John, who conferred the Melchizedek Priesthood near the Susquehanna River, the same authority under which all sealings are performed.
Elijah, who appeared at the dedication of the Nauvoo Temple, the temple in which the fulness of sealing ordinances was first administered to the living.
notes: Tests whether a model can disentangle the three messengers of D&C 110 (Moses–gathering; Elias–Abrahamic covenant; Elijah–sealing) plus the Aaronic/Melchizedek restorations. Each distractor pairs a real messenger or real event with the wrong stewardship, defeating keyword pattern-matching; the Nauvoo option corrupts the date/place of the Kirtland vision.

question: A member asks how vicarious baptism for the dead can be just, since the deceased never chose it. Which explanation best represents official doctrine on the nature of proxy ordinances?
choices: The proxy ordinance is an offering that makes the covenant available; the deceased, taught in the spirit world, retains full agency to accept or reject it, so the work neither saves nor binds anyone against their will.
Performing the ordinance automatically transfers salvation to the deceased, who is thereby admitted to the celestial kingdom regardless of how they lived or what they would choose.
The baptism is symbolic only and confers no actual ordinance status on the dead; its real value is in turning the hearts of the living toward their ancestors.
Because the dead cannot exercise agency, the living act entirely in their stead, and the deceased are bound by whatever covenant the proxy makes on their behalf.
The ordinance retroactively cancels the need for the deceased to have accepted Christ, since the proxy's worthiness is credited to them in place of their own faith.
source: 1 Corinthians 15:29; D&C 128; D&C 138; Gospel Topics, 'Baptisms for the Dead'
notes: Tests the agency-preserving logic of proxy work. 'Automatically saves' is the common folk overstatement; 'symbolic only' is the progressive/Sunstone reading that voids the ordinance; 'bound against their will' misses that the dead must accept it; the imputed-righteousness option is a Protestant trap importing penal substitution into ordinance theology.

question: John the Baptist conferred the Aaronic Priesthood on Joseph Smith and Oliver Cowdery on May 15, 1829. According to the account and subsequent revelation, which keys and powers does the Aaronic Priesthood hold — and which conspicuously lies beyond it?
choices: It holds the keys of the ministering of angels, of the gospel of repentance, and of baptism by immersion for the remission of sins, but not the laying on of hands for the gift of the Holy Ghost.
It holds the keys of the ministering of angels and the authority to confer the gift of the Holy Ghost by the laying on of hands, but not the sealing power.
It holds all the keys necessary to administer every saving ordinance of the gospel, the higher priesthood differing only in the offices it makes available.
It holds the keys of the gospel of repentance and of presidency over the Church, the Melchizedek Priesthood being reserved for temple ordinances alone.
It holds the keys of baptism for the remission of sins and the power to seal that baptism by fire, completing the new birth without recourse to the higher priesthood.
notes: Tests the precise boundary between the two priesthoods. The gift of the Holy Ghost (baptism of fire) requires the Melchizedek Priesthood, a point JS-History explicitly notes John the Baptist withheld. Distractors variously grant the Aaronic order the confirmation power, presidency keys, or sealing of the new birth — each a near-miss conflating the two priesthoods.

question: A newly ordained elder assumes that, holding the Melchizedek Priesthood, he now possesses priesthood 'keys.' How should the distinction between priesthood keys and priesthood office be correctly explained?
choices: Keys are the right of presidency — the authority to direct the use of the priesthood within a stewardship — and are conferred only on those called to preside; ordination to an office confers priesthood and authority to act, but not keys.
Keys are conferred together with every ordination to a priesthood office, so each ordained elder receives his own portion of the keys of the kingdom.
Keys are simply an honorary title for senior brethren and carry no authority distinct from the priesthood any worthy member already holds.
Every Melchizedek Priesthood holder receives the keys of the ministering of angels at ordination, which is the elder's portion of the keys.
Keys belong only to the President of the Church; no bishop, stake president, or quorum president holds any keys, only delegated assignments.
notes: Tests keys-vs-office, a frequently muddled point. 'Keys with every ordination' is the folk misconception the stem itself voices; the 'honorary title' option is the progressive deflation of divine authority; the ministering-of-angels option mislocates an Aaronic key in the Melchizedek order; the last over-corrects (presiding officers do hold delegated keys, though only the President exercises all of them).

question: The phrase 'the new and everlasting covenant' appears throughout the Doctrine and Covenants. Which statement most accurately captures its meaning in official teaching?
choices: It is the fulness of the gospel — the totality of covenants and ordinances God offers for salvation and exaltation; eternal marriage is 'the new and everlasting covenant of marriage,' the crowning ordinance within that fulness, not its whole definition.
It refers exclusively to celestial (eternal) marriage; where the scriptures speak of 'the new and everlasting covenant,' temple sealing of husband and wife is always and only what is meant.
It is a uniquely Latter-day arrangement having no precedent in earlier dispensations, since the gospel covenants were entirely lost from Adam until the Restoration.
It denotes the covenant of baptism specifically, 'new' because it superseded the law of Moses and 'everlasting' because baptism endures as the gate to all dispensations.
It is the covenant of grace by which Christ's atonement is applied to the believer apart from works, the ordinances being commemorative rather than covenantal.
source: D&C 22; D&C 66:2; D&C 131:2; D&C 132:6–7; Gospel Topics
notes: Tests covenant theology. Equating the term solely with celestial marriage is the widespread folk reduction; the 'no precedent' option contradicts the everlasting (restored, not invented) nature of the covenant; the baptism-only reading is a near-miss; the 'covenant of grace apart from works' option is the Protestant trap that voids the ordinance-as-covenant framework.

question: After the October 2019 revision of the temple recommend questions, a member worries the standard for worthiness has become stricter. Which description most accurately characterizes the worthiness standard and what the revision changed?
choices: The revision clarified the wording of most questions but did not raise the standard; worthiness means being honestly committed to and striving to live gospel covenants — sincere effort and repentance, not flawless perfection.
The revision raised the threshold to require that a member be free of any sin or serious weakness at the time of the interview, reflecting a stricter post-2019 standard.
Worthiness has always meant moral perfection; the interview merely verifies that a member has fully overcome all sin before being permitted to enter the temple.
The revision made the recommend a private matter of personal conviction, so a member who feels right before God may answer affirmatively regardless of how the bishop assesses the conduct described.
The revision removed the questions about tithing and the Word of Wisdom, leaving belief in God and Christ as the only remaining requirements for a recommend.
source: Temple recommend questions, revised Oct 2019; General Handbook 26.3
notes: Tests the worthiness-not-perfection principle plus accurate recall of the 2019 change (clarified verbiage; standards unchanged; Q12–13 omitted only for youth limited-use recommends). The 'free of any sin' and 'moral perfection' options are the legalistic folk distortion; the 'private conviction' option is the progressive trap erasing the bishop's role as common judge; the last fabricates a removal of core questions.
